design_detail: Critical review plus meta-analysis of cross-sectional studies comparing neuropsychological test performance between people with methamphetamine abuse or dependence and normal comparison participants. 18 studies identified (951 participants); one excluded as an outlier, leaving 17 studies (471 users, 445 comparison participants) and 157 effect sizes in 9 domains, pooled with a two-level mixed-effects multivariate model.
can_establish: The average standardized difference in test performance between users and comparison groups in the studies available up to 2006, by cognitive domain.
cannot_establish: That methamphetamine caused the differences (all included studies are cross-sectional; premorbid ability, socioeconomic status and ethnicity were not reported consistently enough to examine, p. 289); how many users are impaired relative to norms; or the effect of abstinence (study-level moderator analysis with few studies).

sample.recruitment: Not applicable (meta-analysis). Included studies averaged 53.9 participants (range 19–130) (p. 284).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Adults 18+; English; users with lifetime methamphetamine abuse or dependence and methamphetamine as primary drug; comparison participants without stimulant dependence or severe neurological or psychiatric illness; methamphetamine not administered by experimenters; at least one standardized neuropsychological test; enough data for effect sizes (p. 281). Criteria described as intentionally liberal; matching and abstinence were not required.
sample.demographics: Users: age 34.6, education 12.5 years, 65% male, mean use 124 months, mean abstinence 295 days (SD 359, range 0–1241). Comparison: age 32.8, education 13.9 years, 62% male (Table 2, p. 284).
sample.selection_effects: Liberal inclusion admits poorly matched and currently using samples (abstinence range starts at 0 days). 76% of studies did not match groups on education (p. 285).

exposure.measurement: As in the primary studies; inconsistently reported (p. 289).
exposure.polysubstance: 6 studies excluded users with prior non-methamphetamine substance disorders and 11 did not; this made no significant difference to effect sizes (p. 286).
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: Mean 295 days across 12 studies reporting it; range 0–1241 days (Table 2, p. 284).

comparison.controls: Normal comparison participants in each study.
comparison.matching: Education matched in a minority (24%) of studies (p. 285).
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Premorbid IQ, socioeconomic status and ethnicity not reported consistently and not analysed (p. 289).

outcomes.instruments: Standardized neuropsychological tests classified into 9 domains by consensus of independent raters (Table 1, p. 283).
outcomes.validity_norms: Group differences only; no normative or impairment-rate analysis.
outcomes.operationalization: Standardized mean difference d (Hedges-corrected), negative = users worse (p. 282).
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: Multivariate model accounts for multiple outcomes per study; moderators tested one at a time without correction (p. 283).

analysis.effect_sizes: Grand mean d=−0.558 (SE 0.034), between-study variance 0.037 (SE 0.012, p<0.01), computed on 18 studies (p. 283; Figure 1 legend). After excluding the outlying research group (d=−1.37), domain means across 17 studies: learning −0.66, executive functions −0.63, memory −0.59, information-processing speed −0.52, motor −0.48, attention/working memory −0.39, visuoconstruction −0.37, language −0.34; simple reaction time's confidence interval included zero (p. 284). Read from Figure 1 (approximate): reaction time about −0.37 (CI about −0.76 to 0.02) (p. 286). Research groups differed significantly in effect size (χ²(10)=30.1, p<0.001), reducing between-study variance to 0.026 (p. 284). Moderators, each tested alone: every 1% more men in the user group made the difference 0.01 SD larger (p<0.001); every year older, 0.04 SD larger (p<0.05); education discrepancy, abstinence and duration of use not significant (pp. 285–286).
analysis.covariates: Single moderators only; too few studies for joint models (p. 283).
analysis.selective_reporting: Publication bias assessed only by visual inspection of a funnel plot (p. 284).
analysis.power: Moderator analyses underpowered (17 studies; acknowledged p. 283).

interpretation_gap.results_show: Across 17 cross-sectional studies up to 2006, users scored on average about half a standard deviation below comparison groups, most in learning, executive function and memory, with substantial between-group heterogeneity and no adjustment for premorbid differences.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The discussion attributes the pattern to methamphetamine-associated frontostriatal neurotoxicity (pp. 286–288, 290–291) and calls MA dependence associated with moderate neuropsychological impairment at the group level (p. 290). The association wording is accurate; the mechanistic attribution goes beyond cross-sectional data. The review also cites Volkow et al. (2001b) as showing psychomotor and memory deficits persisting for at least 9 months in a less severe form (p. 289), which that paper did not test: it compared users with neither controls nor norms and reported non-significant within-user trends.

timeline.event: Critical review argues the group differences are mostly within the normal range
Larger meta-analysis (44 studies) finds similar moderate average deficits and strong publication bias
Meta-analysis restricted to abstinent samples finds smaller, domain-dependent differences
Meta-analysis of 68 later studies finds larger average differences with prediction intervals including zero

replication.where_it_stands: The direction and approximate size of average group differences replicated in later meta-analyses; their cause and clinical meaning remain contested.

funding.declared_conflicts: No conflict-of-interest statement; a disclaimer states the views are not those of the US Navy, Department of Defense or Government (p. 291).
funding.affiliations_note: Several included studies come from the authors' own research centre.

what_would_settle_it: A pre-registered individual-participant meta-analysis with premorbid ability estimates, normative impairment rates, abstinence verified, and a formal risk-of-bias assessment of each study.

domains.note: PubMed, PsycInfo and Web of Science to January 2007, two independent searchers; English only; no search strings or grey literature (p. 282).

domains.domain: List of excluded studies with reasons (critical)
Risk of bias of individual studies (critical)

domains.note: Multivariate mixed-effects model handling multiple outcomes per study.

domains.domain: Risk of bias considered in interpretation (critical)
domains.note: Confounds discussed but not assessed per study.
Visual funnel inspection only; trim-and-fill cited but no result reported.
Review funding reported; included studies' funding not.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: Several critical AMSTAR 2 items fail (no protocol, no excluded-study list, no risk-of-bias assessment), as was common in 2007. The pooled estimate is methodologically sound as an average of what was published, but it averages confounded comparisons.

key_findings.finding: 17 studies, 471 users and 445 comparison participants, 157 effect sizes after excluding one outlying study (18 studies and 951 participants before exclusion).

Domain effect sizes (d): learning −0.66, executive −0.63, memory −0.59, speed −0.52, motor −0.48, attention/working memory −0.39, visuoconstruction −0.37, language −0.34; simple reaction time not significant.
Effect sizes differed significantly by research group (χ²(10)=30.1, p<0.001).
More men in the user sample and older user samples went with larger differences; education discrepancy, abstinence length and duration of use did not significantly moderate effects.
76% of studies did not match groups on education; users averaged 12.5 and comparison participants 13.9 years of education.
Average deficits were larger than meta-analytic estimates for cocaine (d=−0.35) and cannabis (d=−0.15) cited by the authors.
Publication bias judged absent by visual inspection of the funnel plot only.

reporting_issues.issue: The grand mean (d=−0.558) and Figure 1's reference band are computed on 18 studies including the one later excluded, while the domain estimates use 17.
reporting_issues.consequence: The headline overall estimate includes the outlier.

reporting_issues.issue: Volkow et al. (2001b) is cited as showing deficits that persisted at least 9 months in less severe form; that study made no comparison with controls or norms and found non-significant within-user trends.
reporting_issues.consequence: A citation overstates its source; the claim should not be relayed.

reporting_issues.issue: The 40% global impairment figure is attributed to Rippeth et al. (2004) without the subgroup it applies to.
reporting_issues.consequence: Not usable until checked against the primary paper.

verification.source_read: PDF, pp. 275–297 (all pages; Figure 1 read on the rendered page)
